extracted.intended_audience: students, general readers, and practitioners interested in Indian aesthetics, philosophy of art, and classical Indian performing/visual arts
extracted.subtask_description: An expository overview of the classical Indian theory of Rasa: what Rasa means, its central components (Rasa Sutra), the canonical list of Rasas, key commentators (Bharata, Abhinavagupta), and how the theory applies across art forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa as purified, universalized emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa denotes the aesthetic flavor of a work that evokes an indescribable feeling; it is not the ordinary, personal emotion but a purified, universalized form of that emotion which the audience 'tastes' rather than simply feels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between ordinary, context‑bound emotion (tangled with people and circumstances) and the aesthetic Rasa (purified essence). When crafting or evaluating a work, look for evidence that emotion has been de‑personalized and transformed into an impersonal, universal affective tone rather than diaristic or situational feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must evoke Rasa (Bharata's core claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata's claim: 'no meaningful idea is conveyed if Rasa is not evoked' — art without Rasa is simply empty form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful dramatic/literary/musical work should produce a recognizable aesthetic experience in the audience; technical form alone is insufficient. Evaluate whether the work's elements cohere toward producing a felt aesthetic response rather than merely demonstrating craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical list of Rasas (eight + ninth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata's eight primary Rasas: shringara (erotic/love), karuna (compassion/pathos), raudra (wrath), vira (heroic), hasya (comic), bhayanaka (horrific), bibhatsa (odious), adbhuta (marvelous). Abhinavagupta later added shanta (tranquility/serenity) as a ninth, culminating Rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing, identify which Rasa is intended and whether the work consistently evokes that Rasa. Consider Abhinavagupta's view that shanta can be a culminating aesthetic aim that subsumes other Rasas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa Sutra: vibhava–anubhava–vyabhicharibhava combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata's Rasa Sutra: 'Vibhava–anubhava–vyabhichari-samyogad rasa nishpattih' — Rasa arises from the combination of determinants (vibhava), consequents (anubhava), and transitory emotional states (vyabhicharibhava).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing Rasa requires (a) appropriate objective determinants (vibhava) that set up the emotion, (b) visible manifestations (anubhava) — gestures, expressions, bodily changes — and (c) supporting fleeting states (vyabhicharibhava) that enrich without displacing the dominant emotion. Think of these elements as ingredients that must be balanced (analogy to condiments producing a flavor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vibhava, Anubhava, Vyabhicharibhava defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Vibhava: objective conditions/stimuli producing the underlying permanent emotion; Anubhava: physical manifestations (gestures, facial expressions, bodily changes) that accompany emotion; Vyabhicharibhava: transitory or fleeting emotional states that support and enrich the dominant emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, ensure determinants clearly set the emotional scene, consequents convincingly show the emotion, and transient states are used to nuance without undermining the dominant Rasa. The moonlit river / distant bird / waiting woman example illustrates how suggestion of scene elements can evoke longing without naming it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sahrdaya: the sensitive spectator requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is not available to every observer; the sahrdaya ('one who has heart') is a sensitive spectator who can connect to the work with genuine emotion and possesses the refinement to recognize and relish the crafted emotional flavors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should account for audience receptivity: a work's failure to evoke Rasa in an inattentive viewer does not necessarily mean failure. Consider whether the work presupposes an attentive, culturally attuned audience and whether it offers sufficient cues to engage such a spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer/Artist role: abhinaya and emotional translation
rubrics_metrics.description: The performer (or poet/artist) functions as bearer, medium, and connector of the character's emotions, opening up the Bhava‑Jagat that the sahrdaya enters; mastery of abhinaya (emotional expression through gesture, gaze, movement) is specifically valued for evoking Rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate performers on their ability to translate inner states into the physical signs that engender Rasa in the audience. For creators, cultivate abhinaya or medium‑specific expressive techniques to reliably transmit the intended Rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa resides in spectator's consciousness (Abhinavagupta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abhinavagupta argued that Rasa is a mental state manifested in and experienced by the viewer/reader; the artwork is the occasion but the spectator's consciousness is where Rasa actually comes into being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize design choices that solicit active mental engagement from the audience. Critique should consider whether the work effectively occasions the spectator's internalization of feeling rather than merely portraying it externally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sadharanikarana: universalization / de‑individualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Sadharanikarana is the process by which personal, situational emotions are de‑individualized and universalized, enabling the spectator to transcend personal history and partake in a shared, impersonalized aesthetic experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In composition and evaluation, check for techniques that abstract away from particular biographical detail (so the emotion reads as general human feeling). Avoid excessive personalizing detail that ties the emotion to narrow circumstances and blocks universal resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa as supra‑mundane / spiritually significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Abhinavagupta holds that the Rasa experience can approximate divine bliss (brahmananda); aesthetic delight (ananda) may be a form of spiritual disclosure beyond ordinary experience (lokottara).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work aspires to or attains a transformative, transcendent quality beyond mere entertainment. Consider how formal and affective elements aim toward experiential collapse of subject/object distinctions and the elevation of delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dhvani: suggestion over explicit statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Dhvani (suggestion/resonance) — the idea, elaborated by Anandavardhana and Abhinavagupta, that poetry and other arts should manifest Rasa through suggestion rather than direct statement; meaning resonates beneath the surface of what is said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor indirect, suggestive strategies (imagery, implication, associative detail) that prompt the audience's imagination to complete the emotion. Avoid explicit naming of the emotion; instead craft cues that allow the sahrdaya to infer and taste the Rasa (e.g., sensory scene details that evoke longing without naming 'longing').

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium‑specific techniques to evoke Rasa
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa theory applies across dance, theatre, music, and visual arts: practitioners use abhinaya (gesture/gaze) in dance/theatre, raga selection in music to create mood, and Shilpashastra representational principles in visual arts to invoke specific Rasas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating work, attend to medium‑specific tools (gesture, musical mode, composition, iconography) and whether they are employed in service of a coherent Rasa. The same Rasa may require different techniques in different media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective/shared dimension of Rasa
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is often a collective, shared experience: spectators share and relish the Rasa collectively, achieving hrdaya‑samvada (sympathetic resonance of hearts) and a uniformity of aesthetic consciousness among the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider social and performative contexts in which the work is experienced. Evaluate whether the work fosters communal attunement and shared savoring (e.g., in staged performance, ritual, or communal viewing) rather than only private reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for transformative aesthetic relish over mere representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa theory insists that art's point is not merely to represent reality or demonstrate technical skill, but to produce a specific kind of emotional experience that purifies, universalizes, and can lift the audience beyond the mundane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize measures of transformative impact and experiential depth when judging a work. Technical accomplishment should be assessed insofar as it serves the evocation of Rasa, not as an end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic language as vehicle for aesthetic objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic language operates beyond ordinary language: once absorbed, words become objects of aesthetic experience, allowing suggestion (dhvani) to work and the spectator to complete meaning imaginatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In literary composition and critique, look for language that invites reverberation and associative completion, rather than merely conveying propositional content. Evaluate imagery and linguistic economy that turns description into objects of aesthetic attention.
